title: Feasting together
hookLine: John fasted and Jesus feasted, and critics complained about both: why the Christian year keeps feasts after fasts
tomorrow: Nasruddin lost his key in the house. so why search outside?

lines: JOHN FASTS: HE HATH A DEVIL.
cards: Some weeks are all plain rice and good intentions, and then someone's mom invites you to a dinner that won't end. Here's an odd pair of insults in Matthew's Gospel.
John the Baptist lived on locusts and wild honey, and people said he had a devil.

Jesus came to dinners, and the same crowd called him, in the King James Version, "a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners." Opposite complaints. Why would a holy man get a name for eating?

teach.b: Because the meal was the message. In the Gospels, Jesus eats with tax collectors and people others kept away from, and the table itself says: you're welcome here.
When John's followers ask why his disciples don't fast, he answers with a wedding: "Can the children of the bridechamber mourn, as long as the bridegroom is with them?"
There's a time to fast, and a time when fasting would miss the point, because the guest of honor is here.
The Christian year keeps both rhythms: Lent's fast, then Easter's feast; Advent's waiting, then Christmas dinner. Neither is the holier half. They belong together.
So why the opposite insults? Jesus answers with children in the marketplace who sulk whether the tune is a dance or a dirge: nothing pleases them.
The Gospels show one who fed crowds and sat down with the people nobody invited.
And notice what's tucked inside the insult: the word friend.
On a path of your own, a shared table can be practice too: eat slowly, welcome someone who doesn't usually get asked, and let the meal say what speeches can't.

how: The Christian year pairs fasts with feasts: Lent with Easter, Advent with Christmas. In the Gospels Jesus eats with outsiders, and his critics call him a glutton (Matthew 11:19).

o: a formal banquet held only for honored guests
sharing a big, joyful meal as part of the spiritual life
eating as much as possible before a long fast begins

games.q: fast and feast: tap the pairs.
p: why the disciples don't fast yet

s: in Matthew, critics call Jesus a glutton
"a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners."
the Christian year is all fasting and no feasting
it pairs them: Lent then Easter, Advent then Christmas.
John the Baptist and Jesus were criticized for the same thing
opposite things: John for fasting, Jesus for feasting.

games.q: your church friend is in the middle of a fast when her sister announces an engagement dinner tonight. what fits the bridegroom answer?
o: there's a time to feast: the guest of honor is here, so join the table.
fasting is always holier, so she should sit at the table and eat nothing.
feasting is always better, so she should give up fasting for good.
games.why: Jesus said the wedding guests can't mourn while the bridegroom is with them. fasts and feasts each have their time.

practice: Take one bite of something, or one sip, slowly enough to notice its whole taste. Then picture the person you'd most like at a feast this week, someone who rarely gets invited, and set their place in your mind.

wordCard.voice: Feasting together: a shared table as part of the spiritual life, the feast that follows the fast.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: feast, and set a place for someone who doesn't expect one. Until tomorrow.
